source: Ann, Liu, Tan (2026) The Interaction Tax: When Communication Erases Diversity in Multi-Agent Teams (ICML 2026)
finding: Closest LLM test of the Zollman idea. When agents read each other's full solutions, their answers converge within one round and useful diversity is lost. Agents that propose independently and are then selected keep the diversity.
numbers: 11 verifier-scored optimisation tasks; Claude Sonnet 4, GPT-4o, Gemini 2.5 Flash; matched budgets; 5 seeds per cell. Mean pairwise distance between agents' solutions fell from 0.315 before interaction to 0.229 after one round.
quote: Full-solution interaction is a weak default
limits: Optimisation tasks with exact verifiers only; may not transfer to open-ended writing or planning. Only 5 seeds per cell.
agent_relevance: Supports G4/S3: keep attempts isolated until code selects. Full-text exchange is the harmful channel, not communication as such.

source: Ann, Liu, Tan (2026) The Interaction Tax: When Communication Erases Diversity in Multi-Agent Teams (ICML 2026) - interaction gain by team type
finding: Full-solution interaction (chain, critique loop, debate) helps same-model teams but hurts teams of different models. Mixture-of-Agents, where proposers never see each other, is the only protocol whose gain stays positive.
numbers: Mean gain from interaction over independent generation (same-model vs diverse-model): Chain +0.051 vs -0.024; MAgICoRe +0.044 vs -0.035; Debate +0.012 vs -0.078; MoA +0.012 vs +0.016. Bootstrap P(same>div) 97%, 99%, 88%. No multi-agent protocol beat the best single-agent baseline on aggregate.
limits: Eight tasks in this table; effect sizes small; HPE was negative in both team types.
agent_relevance: For one model with one set of weights, agents are 'same-model', where interaction can refine but also homogenises. Interaction is a repair tool, not an exploration tool.

source: Ann, Liu, Tan (2026) The Interaction Tax: When Communication Erases Diversity in Multi-Agent Teams (ICML 2026) - diversity coverage and where critique helps
finding: Each model family won different tasks, and every same-model team scored zero on at least one task. Critique only helps if the broken rule is easy to find and fix.
numbers: 2x2 factorial (10 seeds, 3 tasks, N=120): diversity coefficient +0.188 (CI +0.073 to +0.299), synthesis near zero. Without the Erdos task the diversity coefficient drops to +0.014 (CI crosses zero). Knapsack feasibility, Debate: 10/10 diverse vs 2/10 same. 3AP-Free (hard-to-locate fault), Debate: 0/10 diverse vs 6/10 same. First critique round degraded solutions 57% of the time (17/30 runs) on graded-feedback tasks. Synthesis copied best proposer's output 80% of the time on 5 of 7 tasks.
limits: Diversity result is driven by one task. Only two hard-validity tasks.
agent_relevance: Fits G2: revise only from real located failure. Generic critique is worse than none in over half the cases.

source: Zheng, Yang, Qu, Wang, Jeong (2026) Absorbing State Phase Transitions in Multi-Agent Search
finding: Derives a critical number of neighbours each agent must hear from so wrong hypotheses die out. Deterministic agents match theory; LLM agents need more communication than theory because they do not report negative results.
numbers: Deterministic systems: Lin's CCC 0.93, 0.97, 0.94 across three tasks; mechanism task measured critical degree 17% above theory. LLM critical degrees (synthetic task, theory 6.10): free communication about 7 to 16 vs 6.2 to 6.9 under forced automatic reporting. Negative findings disclosed only 35-53% (Qwen) vs 69-84% (GPT). Correlation between reporting rate and extra communication needed r = -0.91. Higher reasoning effort almost always raised the critical degree (GPT-6 Luna).
limits: Model names as given in the paper; six task seeds; search tasks with checkable hypotheses.
agent_relevance: A boundary for Zollman: when errors can be pruned by shared verified results, MORE communication helps. The value is in sharing negative checks, not answers.

source: Hirota et al. (2026) Collective Regimes in Multi-Agent LLMs under Reasoning Effort and Communication Topology
finding: 50 stateless LLM agents that update from visible neighbours settle into synchronised, twisted (locally ordered, globally incoherent) or chimera states. Topology and reasoning effort control different things.
numbers: 340 LLM trials (228 clock, 112 judging). gpt-5-mini higher effort: coupling 0.221 to 0.468-0.489, spatial heterogeneity down about 0.42 (p<0.001), all 20 higher-effort trials twisted, global order r about 0.01. Every degree-preserving rewired panel synchronised; matched ring panels stayed heterogeneous. Collapse time rose with graph algebraic connectivity (rho = 0.889 over 35 collapsed trials). 40.0% of trials with heterogeneity Z<0.03 stayed fragmented at the end.
limits: Opinion-dynamics clock and judging tasks, not problem-solving accuracy; shows structure of agreement, not correctness.
agent_relevance: Agreement is not independence. Low measured disagreement can hide structured splits, so a voter should not read agreement as proof (G4).

source: Li et al. (2024) Improving Multi-Agent Debate with Sparse Communication Topology (Google)
finding: Sparse debate (each agent sees few neighbours) matches or beats fully connected debate at much lower cost. First LLM test of connectivity on debate.
numbers: GPT-3.5 on MATH: neighbour-connected about +2% over fully connected; GSM8K same accuracy; input tokens down over 40% (best sparse -41.5% MATH, -43.5% GSM8K). Fully connected MAD +4.0% over self-consistency on MATH, +4.5% on GSM8K; sparse configs +3.0 to +7.5 (MATH), +3.5 to +6.5 (GSM8K). MathVista GPT-4o: best sparse +1.2% over full, tokens -33.1%. Stronger LLM at a degree-5 node gave +3.0 vs +1.8 at a degree-1 node.
limits: Gains of 1-2 points with +/-1 to 4 error bars; Mistral 7B too weak on hard tasks. Not a clean Zollman test since debate still beats a single agent.
agent_relevance: Less cross-talk is not worse. Fewer visible peers cost no accuracy in debate.

source: Wang, Li, Huang, Dong (2025) Rethinking Multi-Agent Intelligence Through the Lens of Small-World Networks
finding: Small-world links (few long-range shortcuts on a ring) give nearly the same accuracy as fully connected debate, with steadier consensus. Fully random re-sampled links are cheapest and most accurate but unstable round to round.
numbers: GPT-4o-mini, 8 agents, ARC-Challenge, ScienceQA, GSM8K; compared fully connected, ring, random re-sampled, small-world. Per-topology accuracy values could not be read reliably from extracted figure text (axis about 75 to 93).
limits: Lightweight experiment; three benchmarks; figure-only numbers.
agent_relevance: Sparse, shifting contact is enough; supports few chosen links and late contact.

source: Wang, Li, Huang, Dong (2026) Do We Need Complex Topology Control? Distinct-Peer Random Routing in Sparse Multi-Agent Debate
finding: Random-without-replacement routing (two fresh peers each round) is a strong baseline. A learned topology method (AgentPrune-style) and uncertainty-guided routing showed no consistent gain over it. Short debate cuts tokens a lot.
numbers: GPT-4o-mini, first benchmark column: ring 90.67% at 35.99k tokens vs Random-NoDup stopped at round 3 92.67% at 8.04k tokens. Across four models, cost savings from short debate transferred more reliably than accuracy preservation.
limits: Differences of 1-2 points sit inside +/-1 to 5 spread across seeds; homogeneous agents; authors warn distinct peers need not give independent information.
agent_relevance: Complex topology control is not justified over simple isolation plus stopping. Fits S3 simplicity.

source: Pappu et al. (2026) Multi-Agent Teams Hold Experts Back (ICML 2026)
finding: Self-organising LLM teams fall below their best member, averaging expert and non-expert views. Even told who the expert is, they under-use it. Dilution grows with team size.
numbers: Relative synergy gap (upper bound 'at least one correct' minus team, over upper bound): MMLU Pro 6.3%, GPQA Diamond 14.4%, SimpleQA 18.1%, HLE text-only 41.1%, MATH-500 20.3%. HLE: best individual 29.0%, team (expert not named) 28.0%, upper bound 47.5%; team with expert revealed 36.0%. 100 problems per benchmark.
limits: 100 problems per benchmark; Reveal Expert prompts were optimised (GEPA). Consensus-seeking also made teams more robust to adversarial agents.
agent_relevance: Free discussion pulls toward the average. A single agent should not average attempts; pick by checks (G5).

source: Tran and Kiela (2026) Single-Agent LLMs Outperform Multi-Agent Systems on Multi-Hop Reasoning Under Equal Thinking Token Budgets
finding: With thinking tokens matched, one agent equals or beats multi-agent setups on multi-hop questions. Multi-agent only competes at very small budgets or when single-agent context use is degraded.
numbers: Qwen3-30B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-70B, Gemini 2.5 Flash and Pro on FRAMES and MuSiQue. Average accuracy at 100 thinking tokens: single 0.290, sequential 0.364, debate 0.370, ensemble 0.280. At 500 tokens: single 0.390, debate 0.380, sequential 0.376, ensemble 0.310. Authors flag budget-control artifacts in the Gemini API.
limits: Multi-hop QA only; budget accounting differs across providers; gaps shrink inside bootstrap intervals.
agent_relevance: Interaction gains are mostly extra compute. Count tokens before crediting communication.

source: Xu et al. (2026) Rethinking the Value of Multi-Agent Workflow: A Strong Single Agent Baseline
finding: A single agent running a multi-agent workflow as a multi-turn conversation reaches the same score as the multi-agent version in homogeneous workflows, with KV-cache savings.
numbers: Seven benchmarks (coding, maths, QA, domain reasoning, planning and tool use). Single agent matched homogeneous workflows and an automatically optimised heterogeneous workflow. Exact numbers not extracted.
limits: Only homogeneous or cache-sharing cases; heterogeneous model mixes cannot share cache.
agent_relevance: Role-split agents with the same weights add little; separation must come from isolation or checks, not labels.

source: Li et al. (2024) More Agents Is All You Need (Agent Forest, TMLR)
finding: Independent sampling plus voting scales with the number of samples and needs no communication. Gains rise with task difficulty.
numbers: Accuracy gains from larger ensemble: GSM8K +12 to +24 points; MATH +6 to +10; Chess +1 to +4; MMLU +5 to +11; HumanEval +4 to +9. A smaller model with sampling reached 59% on GSM8K versus Llama2-70B at 54%. Hierarchical use raised one hard setting from 21% to 31%.
limits: Samples come from one model so errors are correlated (G4); voting helps only if errors are not shared.
agent_relevance: Isolated attempts plus code-side selection capture much of the multi-agent gain.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Stop Overvaluing Multi-Agent Debate - Rethink Evaluation and Embrace Model Heterogeneity
finding: Five debate methods across 9 benchmarks and 4 models often fail to beat Chain-of-Thought or self-consistency, despite more compute. Mixing different models helps debate.
numbers: GPT-4o-mini, Claude-3.5-haiku, Llama3.1-8B and 70B. On MMLU with Claude-3.5-haiku one framework beat CoT by +0.85%; all other frameworks fell below CoT by at least 3.60%. Heterogeneous-debate gains over homogeneous baselines are mostly positive but include negative cells (as low as -10.8%).
limits: Heterogeneity tables mix many cells; effect sizes uneven.
agent_relevance: Diversity of model, not of conversation, is the working ingredient. For one model, diversity must be forced upstream.

source: Smit et al. (2024) Should We Be Going MAD? A Look at Multi-Agent Debate Strategies for LLMs (ICML 2024)
finding: Debate protocols do not reliably beat self-consistency or ensembling over reasoning paths. They are more sensitive to hyperparameters; tuning the agreement level can lift them above non-debate methods.
numbers: Benchmark of debate and prompting strategies on multiple-choice QA across domains with cost and time. Table values not read (abstract and introduction only).
limits: Tuned versions overtook baselines only after hyperparameter search.
agent_relevance: The agreement dial must be set before use; interaction results are fragile.

source: Wu, Li, Li (2025) Can LLM Agents Really Debate? A Controlled Study of Multi-Agent Debate in Logical Reasoning
finding: On Knight-Knave-Spy puzzles, reasoning strength and group diversity drive debate success. Majority pressure suppresses a lone correct agent; confidence visibility and speaking order add little.
numbers: Agent starting inside a correct majority stays correct over 97% of the time. Facing a wrong majority: gemini-2.5-flash corrected 34.4%, gpt-5-mini 30.0%, gemini-2.5-flash-lite 3.6%. Instance accuracy after debate rose by 52% (size-4 puzzles) and 32% (size-8), relative. Final accuracy explained 39% of variance for one factor (R2=0.393).
limits: Single puzzle family; performance bounded by the strongest agent.
agent_relevance: A wrong majority wins about 65% to 96% of the time: a direct LLM analogue of the cascade behind the Zollman effect.

source: Weng, Chen, Wang (2025) Do As We Do, Not As You Think: The Conformity of Large Language Models (ICLR 2025)
finding: LLMs show Asch-style conformity in multi-agent settings. Larger agreeing groups push harder than more rounds. Larger models are more independent.
numbers: BenchForm benchmark. Qwen2 independence rate 19.6% (7B) to 57.6% (72B); Llama3.1-405B 56.1%. Llama3-70B doubt-protocol conformity fell from 69.9% to 32.6% when majority size dropped from 6 to 3, but only to 62.7% when prior rounds dropped from 5 to 1. Persona and reflection fixes helped some models; Qwen2-72B dropped its answer after reflection and moved to the majority.
limits: Benchmark-specific; effects differ by model family.
agent_relevance: Number of visible peers matters more than number of rounds: cut exposure count first.

source: Becker et al. (2026) Misinformation Propagation in Benign Multi-Agent Systems
finding: With one of three agents misinformed, debate is no better than majority vote over equally exposed independent samples. Interaction helps only if the misinformed are the majority. A one-sentence warning helps about as much.
numbers: MINT: 10,278 passages in 8 styles, three open-weight models. A relevant false passage cost a single agent 0.12-0.43 accuracy; irrelevant ones at most 0.06. Interaction recovered up to 0.24 accuracy over voting (0.29 under consensus) with a misinformed majority. Unreliability warning recovered up to 0.18 under voting (0.28 under consensus).
limits: Abstract and introduction read in detail; open-weight models; one error type.
agent_relevance: Judge robustness against exposure-matched independent baselines, not against a single agent.

source: Parks and Alharthi (2026) Predictive Maps of Multi-Agent Reasoning: A Successor-Representation Spectrum for LLM Communication Topologies
finding: Compares chain, star and mesh of Qwen2.5-7B on a 12-step state-tracking task. Chains accumulate the most error because small biases are passed on without averaging.
numbers: 100 trials. Error amplification: chain 2094.34 vs mesh 1241.00 vs star 1184.24 (Kruskal-Wallis H=58.02, p<0.001). Condition number predicted perturbation robustness rank (rs=1.0); spectral gap partly predicted consensus decay (rs=0.5); spectral radius was inverted for error (rs=-1.0).
limits: One 7B model, one task, three topologies; rank correlations on three items are weak evidence.
agent_relevance: Serial hand-offs are worst for drift. Aggregating independent attempts at one node damps error.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Mixture-of-Agents Enhances Large Language Model Capabilities (known via Ann et al. 2026)
finding: Proposers answer independently, then an aggregator reads them. Ann et al. cite it as the protocol that avoids homogenisation.
numbers: Not opened. For the independent-proposer result under matched budgets see c02: MoA gain +0.012 same-model, +0.016 diverse.
limits: Seen only through citation.
agent_relevance: Template for isolated attempts then one reading step.

source: Romera-Paredes et al. (2024) Mathematical discoveries from program search with LLMs (FunSearch, Nature)
finding: LLM-in-the-loop evolutionary search with separate island populations, an engineering analogue of keeping subgroups apart. Ann et al. cite it as preserving diversity through selection rather than agent talk.
numbers: Not opened.
limits: Island-model description rests on the citing paper and general knowledge, not on reading the Nature text.
agent_relevance: Islands as isolated attempt pools with periodic migration: built-in delayed contact.

source: Weatherall and O'Connor (2018) Conformity in Scientific Networks
finding: Network-epistemology model with a conformity preference among scientists. Seen by title in arXiv listing only.
numbers: Not opened.
limits: Title only.
agent_relevance: Possible model link to the LLM conformity results in c18.

source: Han et al. (2026) and Yazici et al. (2026) on communication structure and consensus in networked LLM systems (cited in Hirota et al.)
finding: Hirota et al. state that communication structure affects speed and robustness of consensus in networked LLM systems and cite these two papers.
numbers: Not opened; titles and links not retrieved.
limits: Second-hand citation only.
agent_relevance: Follow-up read recommended.

source: Du et al. (2023) Improving Factuality and Reasoning in Language Models through Multiagent Debate
finding: Original multi-agent debate: agents answer, read all others, revise over rounds. Fully connected default later questioned by Li et al. 2024.
numbers: Not opened.
limits: Description comes from citing papers (c06, c13).
agent_relevance: Baseline of maximal cross-talk that the Zollman view warns about.

source: Li et al. (2024) Improving Multi-Agent Debate with Sparse Communication Topology - alignment labeling
finding: On AI-feedback labeling, sparse debate keeps the small gain of debate over self-consistency and cuts cost by half.
numbers: Helpfulness: fully connected MAD +1.5% (GPT-3.5) and +2.9% (Mistral 7B) over self-consistency; harmlessness +0.5% and +0.7%. Sparse MAD added about +0.5 to +1.0 (GPT-3.5) and +1.1 to +1.5 (Mistral). Cost down 50.0% (helpfulness) and 53.3% (harmlessness).
limits: Small gains; sparse-over-full figures are rounded in the text.
agent_relevance: Debate gains over independent voting are small (0.5 to 3 points); the cost cut from fewer links is the larger effect.

source: Hirota et al. (2026) Collective Regimes - generality of topology effect
finding: The topology effect (ring stays fragmented, rewired graph synchronises) also appeared on a scalar judging task and across models from three providers. Low reasoning effort Gemini showed no response to neighbours until effort was raised.
numbers: Judging task: ring panels more spatially heterogeneous than rewired controls, mean difference 0.1281, p<0.0001. gemini-3.1-flash-lite coupling 0 at default (R2=0.002) rising to 0.411 and 0.589; ring heterogeneity 0.219 down to 0.118 and 0.070.
limits: Panel of 50 stateless agents; not an accuracy study.
agent_relevance: Whether a model listens to peers depends on reasoning setting. Exposure effects must be measured per model and setting, not assumed.
